english: Do you have a baby bed?
japanese: ベビーベッドって、ありますか？
note: tte softens it — you sound like you're wondering, not demanding

english: Could we have a high chair for the meal?
japanese: お食事のとき、ベビーチェアをお願いできますか？
romaji: o-shokuji no toki, bebī chea o onegai dekimasu ka?
note: Say this before mealtime at the ryokan, not mid-seating

english: Could I have some hot water?
japanese: お湯をいただけますか？
note: For warming milk or formula

english: Could we have a few more towels?
japanese: タオルをもう少しいただけますか？
romaji: taoru o mō sukoshi itadakemasu ka?
note: mō sukoshi = a little more — polite, not greedy-sounding

english: Do you have a yukata for children?
japanese: 子ども用の浴衣はありますか？
romaji: kodomo-yō no yukata wa arimasu ka?
note: Most ryokans have these but may not set them out automatically

english: Until what time can we use the large bath?
japanese: 大浴場は何時まで使えますか？
romaji: daiyokujō wa nanji made tsukaemasu ka?
note: Ask on arrival at Yoshiike and Kawane Onsen

english: Do you have a private (family) bath?
japanese: 貸切風呂はありますか？
note: The most useful onsen question with a toddler — sidesteps shared-bath rules. Often needs booking at check-in, sometimes for a fee

english: Two adults, one child — could we have a high chair?
japanese: 大人二人と、子ども一人なんですが、ベビーチェアをお願いできますか？
romaji: otona futari to, kodomo hitori nan desu ga, bebī chea o onegai dekimasu ka?
note: nan desu ga sets context first, then makes the request

english: Do you have a children's menu?
japanese: お子様メニューはありますか？
note: o-ko-sama is the restaurant-level polite word for child

english: A small plate for sharing, please
japanese: 取り分け用のお皿をお願いします
romaji: torikawake-yō no o-sara o onegai shimasu
note: You'll want this at nearly every meal. Say o-sara futatsu for two plates

japanese: 子ども用の食器はありますか？
romaji: kodomo-yō no shokki wa arimasu ka?
note: shokki covers plates, bowls and cutlery. Swap in: o-sara (plate), o-wan (bowl), supūn (spoon), fōku (fork), koppu (cup)
Negative question = more natural than asking 'is this spicy?' directly

japanese: お会計をお願いします
note: More natural than just saying kaikei alone

english: I'd like to get here… [show map]
japanese: ここに行きたいんですが
romaji: koko ni ikitai n desu ga
note: Trail off — the unfinished ga implies 'can you help?'
Casual iranai works too; daijōbu desu is smoothest at a conbini
Toire is universally understood
Useful habit — e.g. Kosaku in Kawaguchiko is cash-only

japanese: レギュラー、満タンでお願いします
note: For full-service stations. Many are self-serve (セルフ). Return the rental full
For reporting a problem. To ASK if you can use one: ETC kādo wa tsukaemasu ka?

japanese: ベビーカー置き場はどこですか？
romaji: bebīkā okiba wa doko desu ka?
note: okiba = storage spot — literally 'place for placing'

english: What's the minimum age for this ride?
japanese: このアトラクションは何歳から乗れますか？
romaji: kono atorakushon wa nansai kara noremasu ka?

note: The most formal 'yes, I'll do it'. Your request has been accepted
Expect this before they fetch something or make a call
gozaimasu is the formal service version of arimasu — same meaning

english: I'm very sorry — we don't have that
note: A deep apology. After a request, this means no

japanese: ただいまお持ちします
note: Said after you've requested something — it's on its way

english: Sorry to have kept you waiting
note: A reflex every time staff return to you — not an apology for a real wait
Heard when being led to a table — just follow

japanese: ご予約はございますか？
note: First thing you'll hear at any mid-range restaurant
Hold up fingers if needed. nan-nin is the less formal version

replyList.r: otona futari to, kodomo hitori desu

japanese: ご注文はお決まりですか？
note: The waiter's cue that they're ready to take your order

japanese: お名前をお聞かせください
note: Heard at ryokan check-in — have your booking name ready

japanese: ただいま満席でございます
note: Restaurant is full. Ask the wait time, or bow and move on

english: Do you have a point card?
japanese: ポイントカードはお持ちですか？
romaji: pointo kādo wa o-mochi desu ka?
note: Asked at nearly every conbini and chain store

japanese: お子さんは何歳ですか？
note: Softer variant: o-ikutsu desu ka. Ages use -sai
Often just otoko no ko? with rising tone

japanese: おむつは取れていますか？
note: Asked at onsen and pools — many baths require children to be toilet-trained
A COMPLIMENT reflex — deflect modestly, like 哪里哪里 / 过奖了

replyList.r: iie, mada benkyō-chū desu. hontō ni sukoshi dake desu
replyList.e: no, still learning — really just a little
no, I've a long way to go

note: A genuine question, not a compliment — answer honestly

replyList.e: I can speak just a little

japanese: ゆっくり話してください
note: Say this the moment they start speaking fast

japanese: もう一度お願いします
note: For when you heard it slowly but still didn't catch it

english: Sorry, I still can't understand — could you say it in English?
japanese: すみません、まだわかりません。英語でお願いできますか？
romaji: sumimasen, mada wakarimasen. eigo de onegai dekimasu ka?
note: The graceful exit after slow/repeat haven't worked
Hotels and Disney staff often can — restaurants less so

japanese: 日本語がわかりません
note: Use after asking for English if none available

english: This one, to take away, please
japanese: これを持ち帰りでお願いします
romaji: kore o mochikaeri de onegai shimasu
note: Say once they've confirmed takeaway is possible

japanese: こちらで召し上がりますか、お持ち帰りですか？
romaji: kochira de o-meshiagari desu ka, o-mochikaeri desu ka?
note: Standard chain-store question. kochira de = for here / eating in
hitotsu = one of a generic item (futatsu=2, mittsu=3). For a named menu item, just say the name then kudasai — e.g. chokorēto pon de ringu, kudasai
matte imasu = the -te imasu 'currently in this state' pattern, same shape as yoyaku shite imasu

english: Is it not ready yet? / It'll be very soon
japanese: まだですか？　もうすぐです
romaji: mada desu ka? / mō sugu desu
note: Either direction — you can ask it, or staff say mō sugu desu in reply

english: I'll go and come back / Go and come back safely
japanese: 行ってきます／行ってらっしゃい
note: Guest says itte kimasu leaving; staff (esp. ryokan) reply itterasshai. A household pairing extended to guests who are staying, not just checked in

japanese: お帰りなさい／ただいま
note: Staff greet a returning guest with o-kaeri nasai; the guest replies tadaima. Same paired logic as itte kimasu/itterasshai

english: Thank you for taking care of us (at checkout)
note: Said leaving after a multi-day stay — warmer and more fitting than plain arigatō, acknowledges the whole stay

japanese: もしもし、[部屋番号]号室の[NAME]ですが
note: moshi moshi is phone-only — never used face-to-face. Standard opener before a phone request

english: Could I have one more pillow?
japanese: 枕をもう一つ いただけますか？
romaji: makura o mō hitotsu itadakemasu ka?
note: onegai dekimasu ka works equally well here — itadakemasu and onegai dekimasu are near-interchangeable for a simple object
-mai = counter for flat things: pillows, sheets, towels, paper
densha (train) + no ('s) + omocha (toy) — literally 'train's toy'

english: You haven't seen my son's toy train, have you?
japanese: 息子の電車のおもちゃを見かけませんでしたか？
romaji: musuko no densha no omocha o mikakemasen deshita ka?
note: Negative-question form sounds softer/more natural than a direct question, same pattern as kore karaku nai desu ka
Literally 'is this a forgotten thing' — the natural way to ask without needing the word 'you' (anata sounds stiff between strangers)

japanese: 忘れ物の届けはありますか？
romaji: wasuremono no todoke wa arimasu ka?
note: todoke = a report/office for reporting something

japanese: 子どもが迷子になりました
note: maigo = lost child (a set term). Say clearly and urgently to any staff member

english: I got the ticket wrong / bought the wrong ticket
note: Lead with sumimasen. machigaeru = to make a mistake

english: Can I exchange it? / change it? / get a refund?
japanese: 交換できますか？／変更できますか？／払い戻しできますか？
romaji: kōkan dekimasu ka? / henkō dekimasu ka? / haraimodoshi dekimasu ka?
note: kōkan=exchange, henkō=change/alter (standard ticketing word), haraimodoshi=refund

japanese: 乗り越し精算お願いします
note: For riding past your paid fare. Most JR stations have a 精算機 seisanki fare-adjustment machine near the gates, no talking needed

english: I'd like to change the Shinkansen time to earlier
japanese: もっと早い時間に変更できますか？
romaji: motto hayai jikan ni henkō dekimasu ka?
note: Preferred phrasing at a ticket counter — henkō is standard ticketing language. Hold up the ticket: kono kippu (this ticket)

english: Please pay the difference / That time is fully booked
japanese: 差額をお支払いください／その時間は満席です
romaji: sashigaku o o-shiharai kudasai / sono jikan wa manseki desu
note: sashigaku = the fare difference. manseki you already know from restaurant reservations

english: Child seat / I have a child seat reserved
japanese: チャイルドシート／チャイルドシートを予約しています
romaji: chairudo shīto / chairudo shīto o yoyaku shite imasu
note: Loanword. jidō shīto is the more formal/legal equivalent term. jūnia shīto is the backless booster for older kids — not needed at toddler age
Japan sizes shoes in cm, not US sizing. US 8.5 men's ≈ 26.5cm, US 8.5 women's ≈ 25.5cm

english: Could you measure my shoe size?
japanese: 靴のサイズを測ってもらえますか？
romaji: kutsu no saizu o hakatte moraemasu ka?
note: Sidesteps the cm conversion — most shops have a foot-measuring tool
haku is the specific verb for wearing things you step into: shoes, pants, skirts — different from kiru for shirts/jackets

english: Can we sit in the very front row?
japanese: 一番前の席に座れますか？
romaji: ichiban mae no seki ni suwaremasu ka?
note: ichiban = number one/the most, so ichiban mae = the very front
Worth asking first — many high-throughput rides assign seats automatically with no choice

english: Waiting for the purple / blue one
japanese: 紫のを待っています／青いのを待っています
romaji: murasaki no o matte imasu / aoi no o matte imasu
note: no stands in for a dropped noun after a colour — 'the [x] one'. ao historically also covers what English calls green (e.g. traffic lights)
shiru (to know) + polite past negative. Different from wakarimasen deshita (didn't understand/realize)
About grasping something, not about an unknown fact — contrast with shirimasen deshita

japanese: 本日はお休みです／今日は休みです
romaji: honjitsu wa o-yasumi desu / kyō wa yasumi desu
note: First is formal, second casual. yasumu = to rest, you already have this verb
Very common between lunch and dinner service — worth recognising on sight

japanese: 必要です／必要ありません
note: For requirements/situations. Use irimasu/irimasen instead for physical objects
zero = everyday use (phone numbers, prices). rei = formal/technical, e.g. temperature
o-heya is the polite form staff use, or when you want to be extra polite yourself
ao historically also covers what English calls green — e.g. traffic lights are ao
hitori and futari (2) are irregular; from 3 up, -nin and the more polite -mei both work (san-nin=san-mei)
